clue.text: Unfinished shroud from 28

parts.note: Odysseus's wife wove a burial cloth by day and unpicked it each night to put off her suitors, so it was never finished; Robert Greene (28) used that weaving as the title of a prose romance of 1587

explanation.surface: A literary reference to a burial cloth left incomplete, taken from the work of another clue's writer.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names the weaving Odysseus's faithful wife never completed, and Greene took it for his book.

clue.text: How to soothe a dog sent to Coventry?

definitions.meaning: a nervous dog is calmed by stroking it again and again, giving it further pats
the Victorian poet Coventry is known by the surname that would follow his first name

explanation.surface: A puzzle about calming a dog that everyone is ignoring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent to Coventry' is the British idiom for being ostracised, but here the poet's first name is Coventry, and the surname is what goes with it.
explanation.definitionFit: Repeated stroking calms a dog; the Angel in the House poet was Coventry by forename, with this surname.

clue.text: Betsy Trotwood would have preferred David to be a great one

definitions.text: Betsy Trotwood would have preferred David to be a great one

parts.words: Betsy Trotwood would have preferred David to be a great one
parts.note: in David Copperfield, his great-aunt Betsey stormed off on learning the baby was a boy, having wanted a girl relative to raise; a girl would have been her brother's daughter's daughter

explanation.surface: A Dickens great-aunt wishing her new relative had turned out otherwise.
explanation.definitionFit: Betsey is David's great-aunt, so a girl in his place would have been her great-niece, a sister's daughter one generation further down.

clue.text: ", said Pnin, lifting two fingers, "has expressed everything about mermaids in only two poems' (Vladimir Nabokov)

definitions.text: ", said Pnin, lifting two fingers, "has expressed everything about mermaids in only two poems' (Vladimir Nabokov)

parts.words: ", said Pnin, lifting two fingers, "has expressed everything about mermaids in only two poems' (Vladimir Nabokov)
parts.note: a quotation from Nabokov's novel Pnin with its opening name left out; the professor credits a Russian Romantic poet with two poems that say all there is to say about mermaids

explanation.surface: A line of Nabokov's novel in which the Russian professor praises a poet's economy on the subject of mermaids.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing name is the Russian Romantic poet whose two poems on rusalki, the water nymphs of Slavic folklore, Pnin admires.

clue.text: Herbert found it insufficient

parts.note: a literary allusion: the poet Herbert judged mere compassion not enough by itself

explanation.surface: A man named Herbert decides something falls short.
explanation.definitionFit: Compassion for another's suffering is the quality the poet Herbert judged not enough on its own.

clue.text: Infantile poet with cavalier attitude?

definitions.meaning: a baby still at the breast is at the most infantile stage
Sir John, the seventeenth-century poet, was one of the Cavalier poets loyal to Charles I

explanation.surface: A childish poet who takes an offhand view of things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cavalier attitude' reads as offhandedness, but it points to the Cavalier poets, the Royalist group of the English Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: An unweaned baby is at the breast, the most infant stage; Sir John of that name was a Royalist Cavalier poet.

clue.text: One happening to be associated with wisdoms by Donald Davie

definitions.meaning: an occurrence, a single thing that takes place

definitions.text: to be associated with wisdoms by Donald Davie
definitions.meaning: the poet Donald Davie titled his 1964 collection with this word plural, paired with Wisdoms

explanation.surface: An occurrence that a poet linked to wisdom.
explanation.definitionFit: An occurrence is a thing that takes place; Davie's collection Events and Wisdoms pairs the plural with wisdoms.

clue.text: In her the —— of all heavenly grace / In chiefe degree are heaped up on hye (Spenser, The Faerie Queene)

definitions.text: In her the —— of all heavenly grace / In chiefe degree are heaped up on hye (Spenser, The Faerie Queene)

parts.words: In her the —— of all heavenly grace / In chiefe degree are heaped up on hye (Spenser, The Faerie Queene)
parts.note: a quotation from Spenser's epic with one word blanked; the missing old word means abundance or wealth, heaped up in the lady praised

explanation.surface: Spenser praising a lady in whom heavenly grace is piled high.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic word for wealth or abundance fills the gap, as the treasures of grace heaped in her.

clue.text: Island folklorist

definitions.meaning: an island of the Outer Hebrides, joined to Lewis, famous for its tweed
Joel Chandler of that surname collected African-American folk tales as the Uncle Remus stories

explanation.surface: Two words: a place in the sea and a collector of folk tales.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hebridean isle known for tweed shares a surname with Joel Chandler, collector of the Uncle Remus folk tales.

clue.text: This time he would not bid me enter/ The exhausted air-bell of ——' (Browning, Christmas-Eve)

definitions.text: This time he would not bid me enter/ The exhausted air-bell of ——' (Browning, Christmas-Eve)

parts.words: This time he would not bid me enter/ The exhausted air-bell of ——' (Browning, Christmas-Eve)
parts.note: a quotation from Browning's poem Christmas-Eve with its last words blanked; the speaker is spared the airless chamber of the reviewer who judges, a phrase also the title of a Sheridan play

explanation.surface: Browning's speaker relieved not to be sent into a stifling chamber.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap is filled by the phrase naming a reviewer, also Sheridan's 1779 comedy title.

clue.text: Boy proceeding by degrees with a shrub

parts.note: Eric, or Little by Little is F. W. Farrar's Victorian school story, so its boy goes forward by degrees

explanation.surface: A boy slowly making his way along with a bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Proceeding by degrees' points to the subtitle 'Little by Little' of Farrar's 1858 novel about a schoolboy.
explanation.definitionFit: Heather belongs to this genus of low evergreen shrubs.

clue.text: His wife refused to turn over a page

definitions.text: His wife refused to turn over a page

parts.words: His wife refused to turn over a page
parts.note: in A Midsummer Night's Dream the fairy queen Titania will not hand over the changeling boy her husband wants as his page

explanation.surface: A wife who won't flip to the next page for her husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn over a page' sounds like reading, but it means hand over a pageboy: the Indian changeling Titania keeps from the fairy king.
explanation.definitionFit: The fairy king of A Midsummer Night's Dream is the husband whose queen refuses him the changeling page.

clue.text: Playwright made the arrows, perhaps, but not the slings

definitions.meaning: John, the Jacobean dramatist who worked with Beaumont and Shakespeare

definitions.text: made the arrows, perhaps, but not the slings
definitions.meaning: an arrow-maker's trade name; Hamlet's 'slings and arrows' are split, since this craftsman makes only the arrows

explanation.surface: A dramatist credited with half of Hamlet's slings and arrows.
explanation.definitionFit: John of that name was a Jacobean dramatist; the word also names the craftsman who makes arrows.

clue.text: Muir's landed property of verse

parts.note: a word for land owned, which Edwin Muir used in the title of his lectures The ___ of Poetry

explanation.surface: A Scottish poet's land holdings made of poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: Landed property is an owner's grounds; Edwin Muir called his lectures on poetry's standing The Estate of Poetry.

clue.text: Some persistent urge, never quite followed, to be a novelist

indicators.note: the part from never comes after the run from persistent urge in the answer
only some of the letters of the phrase persistent urge are taken, a run spanning the two words
never quite means the word never stops short of being whole, its final pair of letters lost

explanation.surface: A lasting urge that was never quite acted upon, leading to a writing career.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes TURGE from 'persistenT URGE'; 'never quite' is NEVER without ER, NEV, and 'followed' puts it after.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivan, author of Fathers and Sons, was a Russian novelist of the nineteenth century.

clue.text: Burden shouldered by Aeneas

parts.note: fleeing burning Troy in the Aeneid, Aeneas carried his aged father on his shoulders

explanation.surface: A load the Trojan hero carried.
explanation.definitionFit: Aeneas's elderly father was carried out of Troy on his son's back, his literal load.

clue.text: Architect sells heath?

parts.note: to hawk goods is to peddle or sell them, typically in the street
a moor is open uncultivated upland, like a heath

explanation.surface: An architect who goes into the business of selling open land.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas of that name was the English Baroque architect of several London churches.

clue.text: Apt to be sighted, say, like a loud dust jacket?

definitions.meaning: sighted sounds like cited, and something apt to be cited is worth repeating
a showy book jacket is covered with blurbs, extracts praising the book

explanation.surface: A book whose garish cover makes it easy to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: A remark worth citing again is memorable; a showy jacket brims with cited praise.

clue.text: His legs dramatically revealed in 1736

parts.note: Les Legs, French for The Legacies, is a one-act comedy staged in 1736 by a French playwright

explanation.surface: A man's limbs exposed on stage in the eighteenth century.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Legs' is not limbs but the French word for bequests, the title of a 1736 comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre de Chamblain, the French dramatist, wrote the comedy Les Legs, first staged in 1736.

clue.text: American writer posted publicity

definitions.meaning: Norman, the novelist of The Naked and the Dead
an advertising leaflet sent through the post

explanation.surface: A US author who puts up notices.
explanation.definitionFit: Norman of that name wrote The Naked and the Dead; the word also means a promotional leaflet sent by post.

clue.text: Proprietors of Churchill play

definitions.meaning: people who possess property or businesses
Caryl Churchill's 1972 play about property and possession

explanation.surface: The holders of a play by Churchill.
explanation.definitionFit: Proprietors are people who possess things; Caryl Churchill's 1972 play about property has this title.

clue.text: Odd as Garfield's affair of Adelaide 8

definitions.meaning: Leon Garfield's children's novel about Adelaide Harris (8) has this adjective in its title

explanation.surface: A peculiar business concerning a woman named Adelaide.
explanation.definitionFit: Odd means peculiar; Leon Garfield wrote The Strange Affair of Adelaide Harris, with 8-down supplying the surname.

clue.text: It was on the cards for Dennis.

definitions.text: It was on the cards for Dennis.

parts.words: It was on the cards for Dennis.
parts.note: Nigel Dennis wrote the satirical novel Cards of ___, about selves assumed and swapped

explanation.surface: Someone named Dennis was always going to get this.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the cards' sounds like the idiom for likely, but it refers to the title of Nigel Dennis's novel Cards of Identity (1955).
explanation.definitionFit: Nigel Dennis's 1955 novel Cards of Identity puts the word on its titular cards.

clue.text: Poet given to concealing love

parts.note: Torquato, the Italian Renaissance poet, was said to have hidden his passion for Leonora d'Este

explanation.surface: A poet who habitually keeps his feelings secret.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of Jerusalem Delivered, by legend, secretly loved the duke's sister Leonora d'Este.

clue.text: Moore heroine associated with Bath healer

definitions.text: Moore heroine associated with Bath healer

parts.words: Moore heroine associated with Bath healer
parts.note: George Moore's novel names its servant heroine with a surname that is also what heals at the Bath spa

explanation.surface: A novel's heroine linked to a medic in the spa town of Bath.
explanation.walkthrough: The heroine's surname is Waters, which is what cures at Bath, the English spa town.
explanation.definitionFit: George Moore's servant heroine is Esther Waters, and the waters of Bath, an English spa, are reputed to heal.

clue.text: Some unusual clothes seen on German poet

indicators.note: only some letters of clothes seen are kept, a run crossing the two words

explanation.surface: A few odd garments are spotted on a German poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes the run from 'clotHES SEen'; 'unusual' only dresses the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Hermann, author of Steppenwolf and Siddhartha, was also a German poet.

clue.text: One of R. D. Laing's sandpipers?

definitions.text: One of R. D. Laing's sandpipers?

parts.words: One of R. D. Laing's sandpipers?
parts.note: the psychiatrist R. D. Laing published a book of tangled dialogues called by this word plural, which also names a kind of wading bird

explanation.surface: Asking which of a psychiatrist's birds is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Laing's book of tangled relationships was titled Knots; the word also names a wading bird of the sandpiper family.

clue.text: Level bet on directions taken by First Lady

indicators.note: the compass letters are picked up by the lady, following her

parts.note: in Genesis Eve is the first woman
N and S are the abbreviations for the compass points north and south

explanation.surface: A wager at even odds on where a president's wife is going.
explanation.definitionFit: Odds at one to one, where the winnings equal the stake, form an even-money bet.

clue.text: Rare poet identified with every man

definitions.text: Rare poet identified with every man

parts.words: Rare poet identified with every man
parts.note: 'O rare' is the epitaph on this poet's tomb in Westminster Abbey, and he wrote Every Man in His Humour

explanation.surface: An unusual poet who represents all men.
explanation.definitionFit: The epitaph 'O rare' marks the Jacobean playwright who wrote Every Man in His Humour.

clue.text: University Wit who spared a groat's worth

definitions.text: University Wit who spared a groat's worth

parts.words: University Wit who spared a groat's worth
parts.note: one of the Elizabethan University Wits, who wrote the pamphlet Greene's Groatsworth of Wit

explanation.surface: A clever graduate who could spare a small coin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Elizabethan dramatist of the University Wits is credited with Groatsworth of Wit, attacking Shakespeare as an upstart crow.
